title: Why QR Codes Have Become a Phishing Tool
summary: QR code scams in Malaysia rose from 223 cases in 2023 to 5,907 in 2025. How QR phishing works, why people fall for it, and how to protect yourself.
body:
QR codes are now part of daily life in Malaysia. We scan them to pay with DuitNow QR, to pay for parking, to open a restaurant menu or to register for an event. That habit is exactly what makes them useful to scammers.

## From the factory floor to everyday payments

The QR (Quick Response) code was invented in 1994 by DENSO WAVE in Japan, originally to track automotive parts during manufacturing [1]. It was designed to be read regardless of orientation, and to stay readable even when part of the code is damaged or covered [2]. The same strengths help attackers. A QR code can be printed, stuck on a wall or sent in an email, and it will still scan.

## What QR phishing is

QR phishing, often called quishing, replaces an ordinary link with a QR code. Scanning the code opens a fake website that asks for login or banking details, or leads to malware that gives a criminal access to the phone [4]. The core problem is simple: people cannot read a QR code. A text link can be checked before it is clicked, but a QR code reveals nothing about where it leads until it has been scanned.

The threat is not new. In 2013, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University studied what they called QRishing [2]. They put up posters with QR codes in 139 locations, and over four weeks the codes were scanned by 225 people who went on to visit the linked websites. Their survey suggested that curiosity is the biggest reason people scan. In a smaller observation experiment, 85% of the people who scanned a code went on to open the link.

## The numbers in Malaysia

According to the Bukit Aman Commercial Crime Investigation Department (CCID), Malaysia recorded 11,919 QR code scam cases with losses of RM80.86 million between January 2023 and June 2026 [3]:

- 2023: 223 cases, RM4.59 million in losses
- 2024: 655 cases, RM6.76 million
- 2025: 5,907 cases, RM40.85 million
- January to June 2026: 5,134 cases, RM28.67 million

The number of cases in 2025 was more than 26 times the number in 2023, and the first six months of 2026 came close to the total for the whole of 2025.

## Common tactics

- A fake QR code sticker placed over a genuine one, for example on a parking meter [4][5].
- A QR code in an email or text message you were not expecting, often urging you to act immediately [5].
- Urgent requests for payment, refunds, prizes or account verification that come with a QR code [3].
- A message claiming that a payment failed and can only be completed by scanning a QR code [4].
- QR codes that lead to app downloads or carry malware [4].

## How to protect yourself

- After scanning, check the web address before you open it, and make sure it is the site you expected [4][5].
- Look closely at physical QR codes for a sticker placed on top of the original [4].
- Do not scan QR codes in emails or text messages you were not expecting, especially codes sent by people you do not know [3][5].
- Do not download apps through a QR code. Use your phone's official app store [4].
- Avoid making payments on a site opened from a QR code. Type in an address you know and trust instead [4].
- Keep your phone's operating system up to date, and protect your accounts with strong passwords and multi-factor authentication [5].
- In Malaysia, if you suspect a scam or have lost money, call the National Scam Response Centre (NSRC) at 997 immediately. You can also check bank accounts, phone numbers and company names on the CCID SemakMule portal [6].

## Why this matters to my research

QR phishing is the focus of my PhD research at the School of Computing, Universiti Utara Malaysia. Most of the advice above depends on people checking every scan themselves, and the Malaysian figures show how often that fails. I will share more about the research here as the work progresses.
